hints: Name the functional group in each structure first, for example A1 is an ester and A2 is a secondary alcohol, B1 is a ketone and B2 is an ester, and so on.
Recall which single functional group in each pair can be oxidised, can form a yellow precipitate with alkaline iodine, can decolourise bromine, or can release gas with carbonate.
For pair A, think about what happens to a secondary alcohol with acidified dichromate or manganate, or with sodium metal, compared to an unreactive ester.
For pair B, think about why $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ responds to the triiodomethane test or to 2,4-DNPH while an ester does not.
For pair C, focus on the difference between a saturated cycloalkane and an unsaturated alkene toward $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$.
For pair D, compare a neutral triol with a molecule containing $\text{-COOH}$ toward $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ or $\text{NaHCO}_3$.
Remember you must use a different reagent for each row, so plan four distinct reagents that each give a clear positive only for one compound.
For each positive result, link the exact colour change or precipitate or effervescence to the correct compound number, A2, B1, C2, D2.
walkthrough:
Sort out what each compound can do**
Look closely at the skeletons. A1 $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ is an ester, it is very resistant to oxidation under mild conditions. A2 $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ is a secondary alcohol, it is easily oxidised to a ketone. That contrast is your key for the first test.

Choose the alcohol test for pair A**
Warm A2 with acidified potassium dichromate. The dichromate ion $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ is a strong oxidiser and is itself reduced: $$ \text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O} $$ You see orange solution turn green as $\text{Cr(VI)}$ becomes $\text{Cr(III)}$. A1 stays orange. Acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ turning from purple to colourless, or $\text{Na}$ giving $\text{H}_2$ effervescence only with the $\text{OH}$ group, are also accepted.

Choose the methyl ketone test for pair B**
B1 $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ contains a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}$ group, B2 $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_3$ does not behave as a methyl ketone. Warm with $\text{I}_2$ in $\text{NaOH}$ and B1 gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane: $$ \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + 3\text{I}_2 + 4\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CHI}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^- + 3\text{I}^- + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} $$ Alternatively 2,4-DNPH gives an orange or red precipitate only with the ketone B1, the ester B2 gives no precipitate.

Choose the unsaturation and acidity tests for pairs C and D**
C1 is cyclopentane, all single bonds, so it does nothing to bromine water. C2 is hex-2-ene, the $\text{C=C}$ adds bromine: $$ \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHC}_3\text{H}_7 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCHBrC}_3\text{H}_7 $$ so orange $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$ turns colourless only with C2. D1 is propane-1,2,3-triol, neutral, so no reaction with carbonate. D2 $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ is a carboxylic acid, so it releases $\text{CO}_2$: $$ 2\text{RCOOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{RCOONa} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} $$ so you see effervescence only with D2.

Final answer: Pair A: reagent acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ (or acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ or $\text{Na}$); positive with A2: orange to green (or purple to colourless, or effervescence of $\text{H}_2$).
Pair B: reagent alkaline $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$ (or 2,4-DNPH); positive with B1: yellow ppt of $\text{CHI}_3$ (or orange-red ppt).
Pair C: reagent $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$; positive with C2: orange to colourless.
Pair D: reagent $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ (or $\text{NaHCO}_3$); positive with D2: effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$.

hints: Decide whether cyclopentane, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$, has any permanent dipole or hydrogen bonding, or whether it is essentially nonpolar.
Link the strength of the only van der Waals force present to the small amount of thermal energy needed for melting and boiling.
walkthrough:
See why cyclopentane cannot have strong attractions**
Draw the pentagon for C1 in your mind. It is just $\text{C}$ and $\text{H}$ with almost identical electronegativities, and the symmetrical ring means any tiny bond dipoles cancel. There is no $\text{O-H}$ or $\text{N-H}$ for hydrogen bonding and no permanent dipole, so molecules attract each other only through momentary uneven electron clouds.

Connect weak forces to low melting and boiling points**
Those momentary attractions are London dispersion forces, also called instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces. They are very weak for a small $\text{C}_5$ molecule. Melting and boiling only need to overcome these weak intermolecular attractions, the strong $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ covalent bonds stay intact, so only a little heating to $-94^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $+49^{\circ}\text{C}$ is enough.

Final answer: C1 is cyclopentane, a nonpolar hydrocarbon.
Only weak London (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole / dispersion) forces exist between molecules, so little energy is needed to separate them, giving low melting and boiling points.

hints: Write C2 as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and place the two H atoms on the same side of the double bond while the two carbon chains are also on the same side.
walkthrough:
Build the cis shape around the stiff double bond**
Number hex-2-ene: C1 is $\text{CH}_3$, C2=C3 is the double bond, C4-C5-C6 is propyl. Because the $\pi$ bond stops rotation, the two groups on each carbon are locked. For cis, put both H atoms on the same side of the $\text{C=C}$ line, which automatically puts $\text{CH}_3$ on C2 and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ on C3 on the same side too. Sketch it as a bent U shape, not a zigzag trans shape.

Final answer: cis-hex-2-ene: $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7$ on same side of $\text{C=C}$, with the two H atoms also on the same side, e.g. $\text{CH}_3$-C(H)=C(H)-$\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_2\text{CH}_3$ with cis H atoms.

hints: Check whether C2 contains a $\text{C=C}$ double bond that can open up and join together with no small molecule lost.
walkthrough:
Recognise the alkene polymerisation route**
C2 is hex-2-ene, an unsaturated monomer with a $\text{C=C}$ bond. When heated gently the $\pi$ bond breaks and each monomer links to the next by new $\text{C-C}$ single bonds, with nothing else formed. That is the definition of addition polymerisation, different from condensation where water or HCl is lost.

hints: Change the $\text{C=C}$ in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHC}_3\text{H}_7$ into a $\text{C-C}$ single bond and add two continuation bonds through the chain.
Keep every substituent on its original carbon: $\text{CH}_3$ and H on the first carbon, H and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ on the second carbon.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond to make the backbone**
Take one molecule $\text{CH}_3$-CH=CH-$\text{C}_3\text{H}_7$ and turn the double line into a single line. Now each of those two carbons has one spare valency to join neighbours. Draw -$\text{C}$-$\text{C}$- with short lines going out left and right through brackets to show it continues.

Attach the side groups exactly as in the monomer**
Do not swap groups. The left carbon came from $\text{CH}_3$CH=, so it keeps $\text{CH}_3$ and H. The right carbon came from =CH$\text{C}_3\text{H}_7$, so it keeps H and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Your repeat unit is therefore -$\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH(C}_3\text{H}_7\text{)-}$, each carbon with four single bonds.

Final answer: Repeat unit: -$\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH(H)(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)-}$ shown with continuation bonds, i.e. $\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH(C}_3\text{H}_7\text{)-}$ with H atoms completing tetravalency.
